scenes.vo: This is a school paddle. Texas law still permits its use.

The school year was twenty twenty-three to twenty twenty-four. Texas public schools reported corporal punishment of five thousand, three hundred and fifty-nine students. That is not a count of incidents. It is a count of children.

overlays.text: Five thousand, three hundred and fifty-nine students

scenes.vo: Eight thousand, five hundred and twenty-eight instances of corporal punishment. Five thousand, three hundred and fifty-nine students. Some were punished more than once. Two hundred and eighty-four districts reported using it.

Texas law defines corporal punishment as “the deliberate infliction of physical pain by hitting, paddling, spanking, slapping, or any other physical force used as a means of discipline.” A board may permit it. Parents may opt out, but must submit a separate signed statement each school year. The board can also prohibit it.

The numbers are falling. In twenty seventeen to twenty eighteen, Texas reported thirteen thousand, eight hundred and ninety-two students receiving corporal punishment. In twenty twenty-one to twenty twenty-two, seven thousand, three hundred and twenty-four. In twenty twenty-three to twenty twenty-four, five thousand, three hundred and fifty-nine. A decline of sixty-one percent in six years. The law still permits it.

In Texas, eighty-three percent of students receiving corporal punishment were boys. Twenty-two percent were students with disabilities. National data from twenty seventeen to twenty eighteen showed Black students were more than twice as likely to receive corporal punishment as white students. Black girls were four times as likely as white girls.

The paddle is meant to change behavior. A review of twenty-one studies, covering sixty-seven thousand, four hundred children, linked school corporal punishment to more aggression, anxiety and depression, and lower school performance. The American Academy of Pediatrics calls physical punishment minimally effective in the short term, and ineffective over time. Its recommendation for schools is clear: abolish it.

overlays.text: Linked to aggression and lower school performance
American Academy of Pediatrics: abolish it

scenes.vo: State law protects school employees, but those protections have limits. Personal liability protection excludes excessive force and negligence resulting in bodily injury to students. Protection from disciplinary proceedings depends on legally justified force: what the adult reasonably believes is necessary, and to what degree. A district may still discipline an employee for violating its corporal punishment policy.
Three hundred Texas districts already prohibit corporal punishment in board policy. Two hundred and ninety-one use exactly the same sentence.

overlays.text: Two hundred and ninety-one use one sentence

scenes.vo: The Board prohibits the use of corporal punishment in the District. One sentence in local board policy. A clear direction for every school employee.

Three hundred and ninety-six districts still permit corporal punishment on paper but reported no use in twenty twenty-three to twenty twenty-four. For those boards, the next step is straightforward. Put that practice into policy. Adopt the sentence. Prohibit corporal punishment.

overlays.text: Permitted on paper. No reported use.

scenes.vo: Find your district's policy at earthpilot dot org, slash kids. Bring the sentence to your board. The Safe Schools Project.
